text: A table-level ACL is a single gate for an entire record on one operation. Can this role read any Incident at all, can it create a new Change Request, can it delete a Problem record. It doesn't know or care about individual fields. Fail the table-level check, and the conversation about individual fields never even starts, because the user never sees the record in the first place.

Table-level ACLs are named table dot operation, so incident.read, incident.write, incident.create, and incident.delete are each their own separate rule. Field-level ACLs are named table dot field instead, things like incident.caller_id or incident.assignment_group, with no verb at all, just the field name. That naming pattern alone is your visual cue, right there in the Access Control list, for exactly which layer you're looking at.

Field-level ACLs are checked in addition to the table-level ACL, never as a substitute for it. That's exactly how a user can open an Incident, see most of the record load normally, table-level read clearly passed, and still find one specific field blank, read-only, or missing entirely. That's a field-level ACL doing precisely what it was designed to do, as a second and fully independent gate.

Picture a contractor role that passes incident.read and incident.write, so it can read and update Incidents generally across the table. But a separate field-level ACL named incident.caller_id requires the itil role specifically, with no contractor role listed anywhere on it. A contractor opens an Incident and sees the short description, the work notes, the state, everything the table-level ACLs allow, but the Caller field simply isn't there.

Nothing is broken in that scenario. Two completely independent ACLs each did their own job: one admitted the contractor into the record, the other kept one sensitive field out of reach. Next, we go one layer deeper into exactly what makes any single ACL pass or fail in the first place, the roles, conditions, and scripts underneath it.
